title: Drug Discovery and Molecular Simulation
answer: Protein structure, new molecules, simulated trials, toxicity forecasting and repurposing.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Protein Structure Prediction
children.blurb: Protein structure prediction is the computational task of taking an amino acid sequence and producing a three dimensional model of how that chain folds.

children.name: Designing New Molecules
children.blurb: Designing new molecules covers the computational work of proposing chemical structures that could become drugs, from small organic compounds to peptides and biologics.

children.name: Simulated Clinical Trials
children.blurb: Simulated clinical trials use computational models of disease, drug action and patient populations to test whether a treatment is likely to work before or alongside human studies.

children.name: Toxicity Forecasting
children.blurb: Toxicity forecasting is the use of computational models to predict whether a chemical or drug candidate will cause harm to the liver, heart, kidney, or other organs before it is tested in animals or people.

children.name: Drug Repurposing
children.blurb: Drug repurposing is the search for new uses for medicines that are already approved or well studied, rather than designing a molecule from scratch.

sections.body: Drug discovery and molecular simulation is the branch of artificial intelligence that works on the chemistry and biology of finding medicines, from the shape of a protein to the behaviour of a candidate compound in a simulated body. In practice, models now predict the three dimensional structure of proteins from their amino acid sequence, propose molecules that fit a chosen target, and screen vast chemical libraries for likely activity before anything is made in a lab. Toxicity models flag compounds that may harm the liver, heart or other organs, and repurposing work searches existing drugs for new uses. The aim is to shorten the long, expensive front end of development, where most candidates fail before they ever reach a patient.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Protein structure prediction is the most mature area, with accurate folds for many single proteins and growing coverage of complexes, though dynamic motion and the effects of the cellular environment remain hard. Molecule design generates plausible structures readily, but predicting whether a molecule will be safe, soluble and manufacturable is still unreliable, and wet lab validation remains the bottleneck. Simulated clinical trials can model how a drug moves through a population and help design real trials, yet they cannot substitute for human evidence, and regulators treat them as supporting tools rather than proof. Toxicity forecasting catches some signals but suffers from sparse and biased data, so false positives and missed effects both occur. Repurposing has produced genuine leads, but confirming them still requires the same rigorous trials as any new drug.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here follow the path a candidate takes from target to second life. Protein Structure Prediction is the starting point, explaining how models infer shape and what that shape enables. Designing New Molecules builds on it, covering generative and screening methods that propose compounds against a target. Simulated Clinical Trials then looks at how those compounds are modelled in virtual patients and how such simulations inform real study design. Toxicity Forecasting sits alongside as the safety check, describing how models estimate harm and where their data limits bite. Drug Repurposing closes the set by applying the same tools to medicines already approved, asking whether an existing drug might work somewhere new. A reader can move through them in order or jump to the stage that matches their question.
